elements.quote: This systematic review aimed to synthesise evidence of the longitudinal associations between childhood and adolescent leisure-time physical activity on adulthood physical activity behaviours and health outcomes.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly labels the work as a systematic review.

elements.quote: This systematic review aimed to synthesise evidence of the longitudinal associations between childhood and adolescent leisure-time physical activity on adulthood physical activity behaviours and health outcomes.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a clear statement of the main objective/review question.

elements.quote: English, peer-reviewed observational studies with a minimum of two timepoints of data collection were eligible for inclusion. We included studies that investigated the association between participation in leisure-time physical activity types in children and adolescents (i.e., 5-18 years), and physical activity, mental health, or cardiovascular outcomes in adulthood (i.e., ≥ 18 years).
elements.reason: The abstract specifies main inclusion criteria (study design, language, minimum timepoints, age ranges, outcomes) and notes peer-reviewed/English which functions as exclusion of non-peer-reviewed/non-English studies.

elements.quote: A systematic search of the literature was conducted across five databases from inception to July 2022.
elements.reason: The abstract identifies information sources (five databases) and reports the date the search was current (to July 2022).
The abstract does not state the methods used to assess risk of bias; while risk of bias methods (modified NOS) are reported elsewhere, they are not specified in the abstract text.

The abstract does not describe the methods used to present or synthesise results (e.g., narrative synthesis approach or statistical methods); it reports findings but not the synthesis methods in the abstract.

elements.quote: Fourteen studies were included in the review, totalling 34,388 observations across five countries.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies and total observations/participants and mentions broad characteristics (across five countries).

elements.quote: Running in adolescence was associated with increased adulthood physical activity in both sexes, while sports involvement was associated with an increase in physical activity in males only. Adolescent team sports participation was associated with reduced odds of early adulthood depression, with varying findings for anxiety disorders.
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for the main outcomes (physical activity and mental health outcomes), describing the direction and nature of associations.

elements.quote: Due to between-study heterogeneity in exposure and outcome measures, a metaanalysis was not feasible in this review, subsequently limiting the ability to present quantitative evidence.
elements.reason: No meta-analysis was conducted; the authors explicitly state a meta-analysis was not feasible, so reporting a summary estimate is not applicable.

elements.quote: Running in adolescence was associated with increased adulthood physical activity in both sexes, while sports involvement was associated with an increase in physical activity in males only.
elements.reason: The abstract compares groups (sexes) and indicates the direction of effect and which group showed the association (males only for sports involvement).
The abstract does not briefly summarise limitations of the included evidence (e.g., risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision); limitations are discussed elsewhere but are not present in the abstract.

elements.quote: Preliminary findings suggest that the lifelong behavioural and health benefits of adolescent participation in leisure-time physical activity appear to be related to the type of activity undertaken, with potential differences between sexes. With the rarity of longitudinal studies spanning from childhood into adulthood, these findings provide important insights for public health strategies to optimise lifelong health and physical activity participation.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of results and their implications for public health strategies.
The abstract does not state the primary source of funding for the review and no funding information appears in the provided abstract text.

elements.quote: Prospero registration CRD42022347792.
elements.reason: The abstract provides the registry name (PROSPERO) and the registration number.

elements.quote: While early PA participation is known to be positively associated with adulthood PA, mental health, and cardiovascular health, the specific activity types that most optimally benefit health outcomes remain unclear.
elements.reason: The introduction describes the current state of knowledge (that early PA is associated with later outcomes) and explicitly identifies an important uncertainty — which specific activity types best benefit health outcomes.

elements.quote: To optimise public health, a better understanding of PA participation behaviours and their relationship with health outcomes is needed. ... Therefore, summarising the current state of knowledge of the longitudinal health and behavioural effects of specific LTPA types could help inform public health policy and direct future research. ... As such, understanding which types of LTPA participation in early life may best promote positive lifelong PA behaviours and outcomes would be beneficial.
elements.reason: The manuscript explains the public health importance and rationale for conducting the review, stating how improved understanding would inform policy, research, and promotion of lifelong activity.

elements.quote: Previous systematic reviews have highlighted the influence of activity structure and type on psychosocial outcomes in children [22] and cardiovascular health in adults [23]. Another review identified a largely positive relationship between overall childhood sport participation and adulthood PA [24]. However, the longitudinal associations between participation in specific LTPA types during childhood and adolescence and adult health and PA behaviours remains unknown. Therefore, this systematic review aims to collate previous findings on the associations between participation in specific types of LTPA in childhood and adolescence, and PA behaviours and mental and cardiovascular health-related outcomes in adulthood.
elements.reason: The authors cite prior systematic reviews and explicitly state that the specific longitudinal associations remain unknown, justifying the need for the current review and positioning it relative to existing reviews.

This review concerns associations between leisure-time physical activity types and later outcomes, not effects of an intervention; no intervention mechanism is proposed in the manuscript, so this item does not apply.
The review does not evaluate a complex intervention or delivery context and does not present or discuss a logic model; therefore this conditional item is not applicable.

No retrieved text explicitly states the review objective(s) or research question(s). The provided chunks include methods, selection criteria, strengths/limitations, and protocol registration but do not contain an explicit Objectives statement or question-formulation framing.

elements.quote: Studies were eligible for inclusion if they met the following criteria: - (ii) observational study design on humans with at least two timepoints of data collection;
elements.reason: The review is of observational cohort studies (not interventions), as evidenced by the selection criteria specifying an 'observational study design' and cohort requirements; therefore PICO-style planned comparisons for intervention effects do not apply.

elements.quote: Studies were eligible for inclusion if they met the following criteria: - (i) Full-text original peer-reviewed journal article published in English; - (ii) observational study design on humans with at least two timepoints of data collection; - (iii) cohort from the general population, - (iv) measurement of at least one specific type of LTPA (e.g., tennis, walking, strength-training), or grouping of specific types of LTPA with similar attributes (e.g., team sports, ball sports), in childhood or adolescence (aged 5-18 years); - (v) quantitative assessment of at least one mental health outcome (e.g., depression or anxiety symptoms/ diagnosis), cardiovascular health outcome (e.g., BMI, waist circumference, cholesterol, cardiovascular events/disease), or PA outcome in adulthood (aged 18 + years).
elements.reason: The chunk lists detailed study characteristics used to determine eligibility: publication type/language, study design (observational, at least two timepoints), population (general population cohort, ages 5-18 for exposures, adulthood 18+ for outcomes), types of exposures (specific LTPA types or grouped types), and eligible outcomes.

elements.quote: Studies were eligible for inclusion if they met the following criteria: - (i) Full-text original peer-reviewed journal article published in English; ... No date restrictions were imposed on the search.
elements.reason: The chunk explicitly states report characteristics: inclusion limited to full-text peer-reviewed journal articles published in English and also states that no date restrictions were applied.

elements.quote:
Reports excluded (n = 93): 
• No analysis of specific types of PA as exposure (n = 49)
• Single timepoint (n = 15)
• Not a peer-reviewed journal article (n = 18)
• Wrong outcomes (n = 5)
• Outside age range (n = 3)
• Specialised population (n = 1)
• Could not locate full text (n = 2)
elements.reason: Although reasons for exclusion at full-text are listed, there is no explicit distinction provided in the evidence between excluding studies because outcomes were not measured versus excluding because outcome results were not reported.

elements.quote: Data from the included studies were collated by narrative synthesis due to the methodological and analytical differences present between studies.

elements.quote: Studies were eligible for inclusion in the review if they were peer-reviewed and published in English; therefore, relevant grey literature and non-English studies may have been excluded.

elements.quote: Studies for inclusion in the review were identified by a single researcher searching electronic databases from inception to 27 July 2022.

elements.quote: Studies were eligible for inclusion if they met the following criteria: - (i) Full-text original peer-reviewed journal article published in English; - (ii) observational study design on humans with at least two timepoints of data collection; - (iii) cohort from the general population, - (iv) measurement of at least one specific type of LTPA (e.g., tennis, walking, strength-training), or grouping of specific types of LTPA with similar attributes (e.g., team sports, ball sports), in childhood or adolescence (aged 5-18 years); - (v) quantitative assessment of at least one mental health outcome (e.g., depression or anxiety symptoms/ diagnosis), cardiovascular health outcome (e.g., BMI, waist circumference, cholesterol, cardiovascular events/disease), or PA outcome in adulthood (aged 18 + years). No date restrictions were imposed on the search.
